A video circulating on social media has sparked considerable attention in Brazil, particularly in Porto Alegre, after a man claimed that his wife, who died of cancer, was officially recorded by a hospital as a COVID-19 death. The video, recorded outside a local hospital, shows the visibly upset man asserting that the cause of death on his wife’s certificate was listed as COVID-19 despite her well-documented cancer battle. This claim has fueled public concern and debate over the transparency and accuracy of COVID-19 death reporting in the region.

To understand the veracity of this claim, it is essential to consider the broader context. Since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, questions about death certification have surfaced globally. Hospitals and health authorities have followed protocols issued by the World Health Organization and national health agencies, which often instruct that deaths of patients who test positive for COVID-19 be recorded as COVID-19 deaths, even if underlying conditions, such as cancer, are present. This policy aims to track the full impact of the virus, as it can exacerbate pre-existing illnesses and contribute to mortality.

In the video, the man alleges that his wife’s diagnosis and treatment history for cancer were well-known to her medical team. He expresses frustration that, according to him, the hospital attributed her death to COVID-19, which he believes misrepresents the actual cause. He does not show the death certificate in the video, and there is no direct evidence presented within the footage to confirm the hospital’s rationale or the details of the certificate.

Hospital authorities in Porto Alegre, when questioned about such cases, have stated that death certificates are filled out based on the clinical course of the patient, laboratory results, and national guidelines. If a patient with advanced cancer contracts COVID-19 and their health deteriorates rapidly after infection, both conditions may be listed on the certificate, with COVID-19 as a contributing or primary cause if it played a significant role in the patient’s decline.

Fact-checking analysis reveals that while individual cases can be complex and emotionally charged, there is no widespread, verified evidence suggesting hospitals in Porto Alegre or elsewhere in Brazil are systematically reporting non-COVID-19 deaths as COVID-19 for financial or statistical reasons. Health professionals face the challenge of determining the primary cause of death when multiple serious illnesses are present. In cases where a patient with cancer contracts COVID-19 and dies, it is medically reasonable for COVID-19 to appear on the death certificate if it contributed to the outcome.

In summary, the video highlights the grief and frustration experienced by families during a complex health crisis, but it does not independently substantiate the claim that the hospital falsely classified a cancer death as a COVID-19 death. Without access to the death certificate or medical records, and given standard protocols for death reporting, the hospital’s actions appear consistent with national and international guidelines. The core claim remains unproven based on the available evidence.

Për të kuptuar saktësinë e këtij pohimi, është e domosdoshme të konsiderohet konteksti i gjerë. Nga fillimi i pandemisë së koronavirusit, janë dukuri pyetje në lidhje me certifikimin e vdekjeve në të gjithë botën. Spitalët dhe autoritetet shëndetësore janë ndjekur protokollat e publikuuar nga Organizata Botëro e Shëndetësisë dhe agjencitë shëndetësore kombëtare, të cilat në shumë raste janë ndjekur të mësuan që vdekjet e pacientëve që testohen pozitivisht për koronavirusin e shënohen si vdekje nga koronavirusi, edhe nëse janë të pranishme sëmundje të mëdha, si kanceri. Kjo politikë ka qëllim të regjistrojë të gjithë efektin e virusit, sepse ai mund të shkaktojë sëmundje të mëdha të mëparshme dhe të përbëjë në vdekje.

Në video, vëllai pohon se diagnostikuari dhe historiku i trajtimit të bashkëshortës së tij për kancerin ishte të njohur nga ekipi i saj shëndetësor. Ai shpreh frustrimin që, sipas tij, spitali ka përgjegjësuar vdekjen e saj si koronavirusi, të cilën ai mendon se e shkakton të saktës. Ai nuk tregon certifikatën e vdekjes në video, dhe nuk ka evidencë direkte në këtë film për të konfirmuar arsyet e spitalit ose detajet e certifikatës.

Autoritetet e spitalit në Porto Alegre, kur u pyetën në lidhje me këto raste, kanë thënë se certifikatat e vdekjeve janë plotësuar në bazë të lëndës klinike të pacientit, rezultatet e laboratorit dhe normave kombëtare. Nëse një pacient me kancer të avancuar kontraktë koronavirusin dhe shëndetia e tij shkon në të rëndë të shpejtë pas infeksionit, të dy sëmundjet mund të shënohen në certifikatë, me koronavirusin si arsye e përbësuese ose primare nëse ka luajtur rol të madh në degradimin e pacientit.

Analiza e verifikimit të fakteve shfaq se, të gjitha rastet individuale mund të jenë të komplikuara dhe të emocionale, por nuk ka evidencë e përsëritur që spitalët në Porto Alegre ose në të gjithë Brazilitë janë në gjendje të regjistrojnë vdekjet e pacientëve të cilët nuk janë nga koronavirusi si vdekje nga koronavirusi për arsye financiare ose statistike. Profesionalët shëndetësorë kanë lëndë të vështirë për të determinuar arsyen primare të vdekjes kur janë të pranishme sëmundje të mëdha. A recent social media post has sparked widespread attention with the claim that “scientists develop a vaccine that cures COVID-19 in three days.” This statement has generated significant interest and hope, but also confusion and skepticism. To assess its accuracy, we explore the facts behind COVID-19 vaccines, their intended purpose, and the scientific process involved in developing treatments for infectious diseases.

COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, first emerged in late 2019 and quickly escalated into a global pandemic. In response, the scientific community mobilized to develop vaccines at unprecedented speed. Several vaccines, including those by Pfizer-BioNTech, Moderna, AstraZeneca, and Johnson & Johnson, have been authorized for emergency use or full approval in numerous countries. The primary goal of these vaccines is to train the immune system to recognize and fight off the virus, thereby reducing the risk of severe illness, hospitalization, and death.

It is important to distinguish between the terms “vaccine” and “cure.” Vaccines are preventive interventions that stimulate an immune response before exposure or early in infection, whereas a cure refers to a treatment that eliminates an established disease. None of the currently available COVID-19 vaccines are designed to cure active infections. Instead, they work by preventing infection or mitigating its severity. Once a person contracts COVID-19, supportive therapies and antiviral medications may be used, but there is no vaccine that reverses an established infection within three days.

The process of vaccine development is complex and highly regulated. Before a vaccine reaches the public, it undergoes rigorous laboratory testing, clinical trials, and review by regulatory agencies. These trials measure the vaccine’s effectiveness in preventing disease and monitor for any adverse effects. The timeline for developing, testing, and approving a vaccine typically spans months to years, even under accelerated conditions. Claims of a newly developed vaccine curing COVID-19 in just three days do not align with established scientific practices or the current state of COVID-19 research.

Additionally, there have been no credible announcements from scientific communities, pharmaceutical companies, or health authorities reporting the development of a COVID-19 vaccine with curative properties or rapid action within three days. Treatments such as antiviral drugs (for example, Paxlovid) have been authorized to reduce the severity and duration of symptoms, but these are not vaccines and do not “cure” the disease instantly.

In summary, the social media post claiming that scientists have developed a vaccine that cures COVID-19 in three days is not supported by scientific evidence or public health announcements. COVID-19 vaccines are preventive tools, not cures, and no vaccine currently exists that can eliminate an active infection in such a short timeframe. Misinformation of this nature can contribute to misunderstanding and false expectations about available medical interventions. For accurate information, it is advised to consult official sources and healthcare professionals.

In a recent social media post, São Paulo’s governor João Doria is quoted as saying that “215 countries have cases of COVID-19.” The post goes on to claim that, since there are only 193 countries in the world, Doria’s statement is evidence that the numbers surrounding the pandemic are fabricated. This claim warrants a detailed fact-check, both of the governor’s statement and the assertion regarding the official count of countries.

To begin, it is important to clarify what is meant by “countries.” The most widely recognized list is that of the United Nations, which has 193 member states. There are also two observer states: the Holy See (Vatican City) and Palestine, bringing the total to 195. Some organizations and lists may include additional territories, dependencies, or partially recognized states such as Taiwan, Kosovo, or Western Sahara, but even with these, the number of sovereign states rarely exceeds 200.

So where does the number 215 come from? During the early stages of the pandemic, various health organizations and news outlets reported COVID-19 cases in “countries and territories.” The World Health Organization, for example, reported cases in “countries, areas, or territories” to account for locations that are not recognized as independent countries but still have distinct governments or administrative systems. These include places like Hong Kong, Macau, Puerto Rico, Greenland, and French Polynesia, among others. By including these territories, the total number of entities reporting cases can exceed the number of UN-recognized countries.

It is not uncommon in public health to use the term “country” loosely to refer to both countries and territories. This is especially true in global reporting, where the aim is to provide a comprehensive picture of the pandemic’s spread. When Governor Doria referenced “215 countries,” he was likely citing figures from international organizations or media outlets that use a broader definition, counting territories and regions in addition to sovereign states.

Does this mean that the numbers are “made up,” as the social media post suggests? The assertion misinterprets the data reporting practices. The pandemic numbers are compiled from a wide array of sources, including national governments and regional health authorities. While the use of “countries” may be technically imprecise, it does not indicate fabrication or intentional deception. Instead, it reflects the complexity of global reporting and the need to account for all affected regions, regardless of their political status.

In summary, Governor Doria’s statement that 215 “countries” have reported COVID-19 cases is not evidence that the numbers are fabricated. Rather, it highlights a common practice in international reporting: including territories and regions alongside sovereign states in public health data. The confusion stems from differing definitions and the loose use of terminology, not from any effort to mislead the public. While accuracy in language is important, the underlying numbers reflect the real and widespread impact of COVID-19 across the globe.

A claim circulating on social media suggests that deaths in Brazil caused by pneumonia are routinely registered as COVID-19 fatalities. This assertion has sparked concerns about the accuracy of Brazil’s official COVID-19 mortality data and the integrity of public health reporting. To assess the validity of this claim, it is important to examine how causes of death are classified in Brazil, the procedures for diagnosing COVID-19, and whether there is evidence to support systematic misclassification.

When the COVID-19 pandemic began, many countries faced significant challenges in differentiating deaths caused by the novel coronavirus from those caused by other respiratory illnesses, such as pneumonia or influenza. Both COVID-19 and pneumonia can result in similar clinical outcomes, particularly in vulnerable populations like the elderly or those with pre-existing health conditions. In Brazil, the Ministry of Health established protocols for reporting and classifying deaths related to COVID-19. These protocols align with international guidelines from the World Health Organization, which recommend that deaths should be registered as COVID-19 only if there is laboratory confirmation or, in certain cases, a strong clinical suspicion based on symptoms and exposure history.

Pneumonia is a common complication of COVID-19, and many COVID-19 fatalities are accompanied by pneumonia. In these cases, COVID-19 is considered the underlying cause, while pneumonia is listed as a secondary condition or consequence. This practice is consistent with international standards for death certification, which prioritize identifying the initiating disease process. Therefore, when a patient who tested positive for COVID-19 dies from pneumonia, the death is legitimately attributed to COVID-19 as the root cause.

However, the claim implies that deaths from pneumonia unrelated to COVID-19 are being registered as COVID-19 deaths. Available evidence from health authorities and epidemiological studies has not substantiated widespread misclassification of pneumonia deaths as COVID-19 fatalities in Brazil. While early in the pandemic, limited testing capacity occasionally led to deaths being classified as “suspected COVID-19” based on clinical assessment, these cases were typically reviewed and updated when laboratory results became available. As testing capacity increased, the accuracy of death classification improved.

There have been isolated reports of inconsistencies in death registration, as is possible in any large-scale health crisis. However, Brazilian health authorities have implemented auditing and verification processes to minimize errors in mortality data. These processes include reviewing death certificates, cross-checking laboratory results, and updating records as new information becomes available.

In summary, current procedures in Brazil do not support the claim that deaths from pneumonia are routinely registered as COVID-19. Most COVID-19 deaths involve pneumonia as a complication, which is why both appear on death certificates. Deaths from pneumonia without any link to COVID-19 are typically reported as such. While data collection during a pandemic is complex and some errors may occur, there is no substantial evidence of systematic misclassification in Brazil’s official statistics. The claim exaggerates concerns about data integrity and does not reflect established reporting practices in the country.

A recent social media post has been circulating widely, claiming that consuming orange, lemon, and honey can prevent infection from the coronavirus. This message has resonated with many seeking natural remedies to protect themselves during the ongoing COVID-19 pandemic. However, it is important to scrutinize such claims with a critical perspective and examine what current medical understanding tells us about the effectiveness of these foods in preventing COVID-19.

The core claim at hand is that orange, lemon, and honey can act as a preventive measure against coronavirus infection. Oranges and lemons are well-known for being high in vitamin C, an essential nutrient that contributes to the proper functioning of the immune system. Honey, on the other hand, is commonly regarded as a natural remedy for soothing sore throats and coughs, and it possesses mild antibacterial properties.

While a healthy diet is undeniably important in supporting overall immune function, there is no scientific evidence to suggest that consuming any specific food or combination of foods, including orange, lemon, and honey, can prevent infection by the coronavirus. COVID-19, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, is primarily transmitted through respiratory droplets when an infected person coughs, sneezes, or talks. The most effective ways to reduce the risk of infection continue to be vaccination, wearing masks in crowded or enclosed public spaces, practicing good hand hygiene, and maintaining physical distance from others.

Vitamin C, found abundantly in oranges and lemons, plays a role in immune defense, but research has not demonstrated that taking extra vitamin C can prevent COVID-19 or any other viral infection. Similarly, while honey can provide symptomatic relief for sore throats, it does not have antiviral properties that would protect against the coronavirus. No credible health authorities or medical organizations recommend these foods as substitutes for proven preventive measures.

It is understandable why such claims gain traction on social media. Natural remedies are often viewed as safe, accessible, and without side effects. While including fruits like oranges and lemons and moderate amounts of honey in your diet can contribute to overall health, relying on these foods to prevent COVID-19 can provide a false sense of security. This may inadvertently lead people to neglect more effective, scientifically supported methods of protection.

In summary, while a balanced diet rich in fruits and other nutrients supports general health and immune function, there is no evidence that eating orange, lemon, and honey can prevent coronavirus infection. The most effective ways to protect oneself remain vaccination, mask-wearing, hand hygiene, and following public health guidelines. It is crucial to base health decisions on reliable information and not be misled by unsubstantiated claims circulating online.

முக்கியமான வாதம் இது: நார்ட்டில், லீமன் மற்றும் ஹனி கொரோனா வைரஸ் பரவலை தடுக்கும் தடுப்பு முறையாக செயல்படும். நார்ட்டில் மற்றும் லீமன் இரண்டும் விட்டமின் C கொண்டவை என்பது பொதுவாக அறியப்படும் உண்மை. இந்த விட்டமின் C என்பது இரத்த மண்ணின் சரியான செயல்பாட்டிற்கு தேவையான ஒரு முக்கிய போதியல் பொருள் ஆகும். மற்றும் ஹனி என்பது குறிப்பாக வாய்க்கு வேதியியல் போதியல் மற்றும் சோர்வு தணிப்புக்கு பயன்படுத்தப்படும் இயற்கை மருந்து என்பது பொதுவாக அறியப்படும் உண்மை. இது மென்மையான ஆன்டி-பாக்டீரியல் பண்புகள் கொண்டது.

ஒரு ஆரோக்கியமான உணவு முக்கியமானது என்பது சரியான தகவல். ஆனால் கொரோனா வைரஸ் பரவலை தடுக்க ஒரு குறிப்பிட்ட உணவு அல்லது அதன் கலவையான நார்ட்டில், லீமன் மற்றும் ஹனி என்பது குறித்து எந்த அறிவியல் ஆதாரமும் இல்லை. கொரோனா வைரஸ் காரணமாக ஏற்படும் கொரோனாவைச் சந்திக்கும் முறை முக்கியமாக மூச்சு செல்லும் தொடர்புடைய திரவங்கள் மூலம் ஒரு பாதிக்கப்பட்ட மனிதன் சிரித்து அல்லது பேசும்போது பரவும். பரவலை தடுக்கும் மிகவும் செயல்பாட்டு முறைகள் தற்போது தடுப்பு போட்டு விட்டு பெரும் மக்கள் தொகையில் இருக்கும் இடங்களில் மறைந்து பேசுவதற்கு மற்றும் கை சுத்திகரிப்பு மற்றும் மற்றவர்களிடம் இருந்து தூரம் வைத்திருப்பது ஆகியவை.

நார்ட்டில் மற்றும் லீமன் மூலம் கிடைக்கும் விட்டமின் C இரத்த மண்ணின் பாதுகாப்பு மற்றும் செயல்பாட்டு போதியலுக்கு உதவும். ஆனால் விட்டமின் C இன் அதிக அளவு கொண்டு கொரோனாவை அல்லது ஏதேனும் ஒரு வைரஸ் பரவலை தடுக்க முடியாது என்று ஆராய்ச்சி காட்டியுள்ளது. ஒரு பக்கத்தில் ஹனி வாய்க்கு வேதியியல் போதியலுக்கு சில நிலைகளில் உதவும். ஆனால் இது கொரோனா வைரஸை எதிர்க்கும் வைரல் பண்புகள் கொண்டது அல்ல. இந்த கொரோனாவை எதிர்க்க உதவும் வகையில் சர்வதேச ஆரோக்கிய அதிகாரிகள் அல்லது மருத்துவ அமைப்புகள் இந்த உணவுகளை பயன்படுத்த விரும்புவதில்லை.

சமூக வலைதளங்களில் இந்த வாதங்கள் என்னென்ன காரணங்களால் பரவுகின்றன என்பது புரியும். இயற்கை மருந்துகள் மிகவும் பாதுகாப்பானது, கிடைக்கக் கூடியது மற்றும் காயங்களை உண்டாக்காதது என்று பொதுவாக கருதப்படுகின்றன. ஆனால் நார்ட்டில் மற்றும் லீமன் போன்ற பழங்களை மற்றும் ஹனியின் குறைந்த அளவை உண்ணுவது மொத்த ஆரோக்கியத்திற்கு பங்களிக்கும். ஆனால் இந்த உணவுகளை கொரோனாவை தடுக்க முடியும் என்று நம்பினால் அது தவறான பாதுகாப்பு அணுகுமுறையை உருவாக்கும். இது மக்களை தற்போதைய அறிவு மற்றும் செயல்பாட்டு முறைகளை மறந்து விடுவதற்கு வழியாக இருக்கலாம்.

மொத்தமாக சொல்லவே, பழங்கள் மற்றும் மற்ற போதியல் பொருட்களின் சமூகம் மிகவும் ஆரோக்கியமான உணவு போதியலுக்கு தேவையானது என்று கூறப்படுகிறது. ஆனால் நார்ட்டில், லீமன் மற்றும் ஹனி கொரோனா வைரஸ் பரவலை தடுக்க முடியாது என்று எந்த ஆதாரமும் இல்லை. தற்போது மக்களை பாதுகாக்க மிகவும் செயல்பாட்டு முறைகள் தடுப்பு போடுதல், மறைந்து பேசுவதற்கு மற்றும் கை சுத்திகரிப்பு மற்றும் சாமான்ய ஆரோக்கிய இலக்குகளை பின்பற்றுதல். ஆரோக்கியம் குறித்த முடிவுகளை நம்பக்கூடிய தகவலை அடிப்படையாகக் கொண்டு தவறான தகவல்கள் வலைதளத்தில் பரவி வரும் மூலம் மறந்து விடாமல் இருக்க வேண்டும்.
article_summary: Um post nas redes sociais afirma que laranja, limão e mel podem prevenir a infecção pelo coronavírus, mas não há evidências científicas comprovando sua eficácia contra o SARS-CoV-2. Embora esses alimentos contenham nutrientes benéficos, como a vitamina C e propriedades antibacterianas, eles não substituem medidas eficazes como vacinação, higiene das mãos e uso de máscaras. A confiança em informações comprovadas é essencial para evitar apropriações equivocadas de dados científicos.

article_content:
A recent social media post claims that a federal investigation in Fortaleza, Brazil, led to a dramatic 90% decrease in the number of daily recorded deaths. This assertion has generated significant attention and debate online, prompting a closer look at the facts surrounding the investigation and its impact on mortality statistics in the city.

Fortaleza, the capital of the northeastern state of Ceará, has periodically been at the center of public health and law enforcement scrutiny. The city is one of Brazil’s largest urban areas, with a population exceeding 2.6 million people. Like many major Brazilian cities, Fortaleza has faced challenges related to crime, corruption, and public health administration.

The core of the claim revolves around a federal probe into alleged irregularities in the reporting of deaths. Specifically, federal authorities launched an investigation into the practices of local officials responsible for death certification and reporting. Allegations included the manipulation or inflation of death figures, potentially for political or financial gain. According to reports, the investigation uncovered evidence of systemic issues in how deaths were recorded, prompting immediate intervention by federal agencies.

Following the onset of the investigation, a notable drop in the number of daily reported deaths was observed in Fortaleza. Some observers and local media attributed this sharp decline—a reported 90% decrease—to the investigation itself, suggesting that the prior figures had been artificially elevated. The implication was that, with increased oversight and pressure from federal authorities, local officials began reporting more accurate numbers, thus revealing a much lower daily death toll.

However, a closer analysis is needed to evaluate whether the investigation directly caused the reported 90% drop in daily deaths. Typically, such a dramatic change in mortality statistics would be highly unusual, barring a major intervention such as the end of a war, a breakthrough in public health, or the correction of significant data manipulation. In this case, the timing of the decline coincided with the federal intervention, suggesting a strong correlation. Nonetheless, there is no direct evidence to suggest that the actual number of deaths in Fortaleza suddenly dropped by 90%. Instead, the most plausible explanation is that the reporting practices changed—possibly shifting from inflated or erroneous numbers to more accurate documentation.

It is also important to note that changes in administrative processes, rather than real-world mortality, can dramatically affect reported statistics. In regions where record-keeping is subject to political or financial pressures, outside investigations can reveal discrepancies not in the underlying situation, but in how the data has been presented.

In conclusion, while it is true that a federal investigation in Fortaleza was followed by a sharp drop in the number of daily recorded deaths, this decrease likely reflects alterations in reporting practices rather than an actual, sudden reduction in mortality. The claim that the investigation "made" deaths fall by 90% is misleading; it would be more accurate to state that reported deaths fell after improved oversight, revealing potential prior misreporting. The situation underscores the importance of transparent and accurate record-keeping, particularly in matters as significant as mortality statistics.

บทความ:
โพสต์บนโซเชียลมีเดียล่าสุดระบุว่า การสอบสวนระดับรัฐบาลกลางในเมืองฟอร์ตาเลซา ประเทศบราซิล ได้ส่งผลให้อัตราการเสียชีวิตที่บันทึกไว้ในแต่ละวันลดลงอย่างมากถึง 90% ข้ออ้างดังกล่าวได้รับความสนใจและถูกถกเถียงอย่างกว้างขวางในโลกออนไลน์ ส่งผลให้เกิดการตรวจสอบข้อมูลที่เกี่ยวข้องกับการสอบสวนและการส่งผลต่อสถิติความเสียชีวิตในเมืองนี้อย่างใกล้ชิด

ฟอร์ตาเลซา ซึ่งเป็นเมืองหลวงของรัฐเซา คารา ทางตอนเหนือตะวันออกของบราซิล ได้รับความสนใจจากสาธารณสุขและหน่วยงานตำรวจเป็นระยะ ในฐานะเมืองขนาดใหญ่ในบราซิล ฟอร์ตาเลซา มีประชากรกว่า 2.6 ล้านคน คล้ายกับเมืองขนาดใหญ่หลายเมืองในบราซิล ฟอร์ตาเลซาเคยเผชิญกับปัญหาด้านอาชญากรรม การทุจริต และการบริหารงานด้านสาธารณสุข

ใจกลางของข้ออ้างนี้เกี่ยวข้องกับการสอบสวนระดับรัฐบาลกลางเกี่ยวกับข้อกล่าวหาเกี่ยวกับความผิดปกติในการรายงานการเสียชีวิต โดยเฉพาะอย่างยิ่ง หน่วยงานรัฐบาลกลางได้เปิดการสอบสวนเกี่ยวกับวิธีปฏิบัติของเจ้าหน้าที่ท้องถิ่นที่รับผิดชอบการออกใบรับรองการเสียชีวิตและการรายงาน ข้อกล่าวหาได้แก่การบิดเบือนหรือการเพิ่มขึ้นของจำนวนการเสียชีวิต อาจเพื่อประโยชน์ทางการเมืองหรือการเงิน ตามรายงาน การสอบสวนได้ค้นพบหลักฐานของปัญหาเชิงระบบในการบันทึกการเสียชีวิต ส่งผลให้หน่วยงานรัฐบาลกลางได้ดำเนินการแทรกแซงทันที

หลังจากการเริ่มต้นของสอบสวน ได้สังเกตเห็นการลดลงอย่างมีนัยสำคัญของจำนวนการเสียชีวิตที่รายงานในแต่ละวันในฟอร์ตาเลซา บางผู้สังเกตการณ์และสื่อท้องถิ่นได้เชื่อมโยงการลดลงอย่างรวดเร็วที่รายงานว่าลดลงถึง 90% ไปกับการสอบสวนโดยตรง ชี้ให้เห็นว่าข้อมูลก่อนหน้านี้อาจถูกบิดเบือนไว้ ความหมายคือ ภายใต้การกำกับดูแลและการกดดันจากหน่วยงานรัฐบาลกลาง ผู้บริหารท้องถิ่นได้เริ่มรายงานตัวเลขที่แม่นยำขึ้น จึงเปิดเผยจำนวนการเสียชีวิตรายวันที่ต่ำกว่ามาก

อย่างไรก็ตาม จำเป็นต้องมีการวิเคราะห์อย่างใกล้ชิดเพื่อประเมินว่าการสอบสวนมีผลโดยตรงต่อการลดลงของจำนวนการเสียชีวิตรายวันที่รายงาน ทั่วไปแล้ว การเปลี่ยนแปลงอย่างรุนแรงในสถิติความเสียชีวิตจะเป็นเรื่องที่ไม่น่าจะเป็นไปได้ ยกเว้นกรณีที่มีการแทรกแซงขนาดใหญ่ เช่น การสิ้นสุดสงคราม การค้นพบความก้าวหน้าด้านสาธารณสุข หรือการแก้ไขข้อมูลที่ถูกบิดเบือนอย่างร้ายแรง ในกรณีนี้ การลดลงของข้อมูลตรงกับการแทรกแซงของรัฐบาลกลาง ซึ่งแสดงถึงความสัมพันธ์ที่แน่นแฟ้น อย่างไรก็ตาม ไม่มีหลักฐานโดยตรงที่บ่งชี้ว่าจำนวนการเสียชีวิตจริงในฟอร์ตาเลซาลดลงอย่างฉับพลันถึง 90% แทนที่จะเป็นไปได้ว่าการเปลี่ยนแปลงการรายงานเป็นสิ่งที่มีความน่าจะเป็นมากกว่า ซึ่งอาจเป็นไปได้ว่าการรายงานเปลี่ยนจากตัวเลขที่บิดเบือนหรือผิดพลาดไปสู่การบันทึกที่แม่นยำมากขึ้น

ยังมีสิ่งสำคัญที่ต้องสังเกตว่าการเปลี่ยนแปลงในกระบวนการบริหารงานสามารถส่งผลกระทบอย่างมากต่อสถิติที่รายงานได้ ไม่ใช่การเปลี่ยนแปลงในสถานการณ์จริง ในพื้นที่ที่การบันทึกข้อมูลมีความเสี่ยงต่อการกดดันทางการเมืองหรือการเงิน การสอบสวนจากภายนอกสามารถเปิดเผยความผิดปกติที่ไม่ได้อยู่ในสถานการณ์พื้นฐาน แต่เป็นการนำเสนอข้อมูลที่ผิดพลาด

article_content:
A claim circulating on social media suggests that boldo tea can prevent COVID-19. This assertion has attracted attention among individuals seeking natural remedies amid ongoing concerns about coronavirus variants and waves of infection. In this article, we examine the origins of this claim, review the scientific evidence, and provide context to help readers make informed decisions.

Boldo (Peumus boldus) is a medicinal shrub native to South America, particularly Chile, whose leaves have traditionally been used in herbal medicine. Boldo tea is commonly consumed for its purported benefits in aiding digestion, supporting liver health, and relieving mild gastrointestinal complaints. Some people believe boldo possesses anti-inflammatory, antioxidant, and antimicrobial properties, which has led to speculation about its usefulness in combating viral infections.

The COVID-19 pandemic, caused by the SARS-CoV-2 virus, has prompted widespread interest in both pharmaceutical and non-pharmaceutical interventions. While vaccines and antiviral medications are the mainstay of COVID-19 prevention and treatment, misinformation and unproven remedies have proliferated online. The claim that boldo tea can prevent COVID-19 fits into this broader trend of seeking alternative health solutions.

To assess the claim that boldo tea prevents COVID-19, it is essential to consider both the traditional uses of boldo and the scientific understanding of viral prevention. Boldo has no established history of use as a preventative measure against viral respiratory illnesses. Its bioactive compounds, such as boldine, have been studied for their effects on liver enzymes and antioxidant activity, but there is no robust evidence that these compounds can prevent the transmission or infection of SARS-CoV-2.

Preventing COVID-19 requires specific interventions targeting the virus. These include vaccines, which stimulate the immune system to recognize and combat SARS-CoV-2, as well as public health measures like mask-wearing, hand hygiene, and social distancing. No reputable health organization has recommended boldo tea, or any herbal tea, as a substitute or supplement for these proven strategies.

Moreover, the suggestion that boldo tea prevents COVID-19 may provide a false sense of security. Individuals who rely on unproven remedies may neglect critical protective behaviors or delay seeking medical care, increasing their risk of infection and severe disease. It is also important to note that boldo tea, when consumed in excess, can cause side effects including liver toxicity and gastrointestinal discomfort.

In summary, while boldo tea is a popular herbal beverage with a long tradition of use for digestive health, there is no scientific evidence supporting the claim that it prevents COVID-19. The virus is effectively prevented through vaccination and other public health measures, not through the consumption of herbal teas. Individuals should be cautious about adopting unproven remedies and rely on guidance from qualified health professionals when making decisions about COVID-19 prevention.

Social media has recently circulated the claim that Intensive Care Units (ICUs) in Rio de Janeiro are being closed due to a lack of patients. This assertion invites scrutiny, particularly given the pivotal role ICUs have played during public health emergencies such as the COVID-19 pandemic and ongoing healthcare needs in Brazil’s most populous cities.

To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is essential to consider both the current state of healthcare infrastructure in Rio de Janeiro and the typical operational procedures for ICU units. ICUs are specialized hospital departments designed to provide intensive treatment and monitoring for seriously ill patients. The number of patients occupying ICU beds can fluctuate based on seasonal health trends, outbreaks of infectious disease, and overall population health.

In Brazil, and specifically in Rio de Janeiro, the COVID-19 pandemic prompted a significant expansion of ICU capacity. Hospitals opened new ICU wards and temporary field hospitals to accommodate surges in severe cases. As infection rates declined and vaccination rates increased, demand for ICU beds associated with COVID-19 naturally decreased. This led to some field hospitals and temporary ICUs closing, as their specific purpose was no longer pressing.

However, the closure of temporary or surplus ICU capacity does not equate to the closure of permanent ICU units due to a lack of patients. Permanent ICUs in general hospitals continue to serve patients with a range of critical needs, such as trauma, heart attacks, strokes, and postoperative care. While there may be periods where the occupancy of these units falls below peak levels—especially outside of pandemic surges—it is unusual for established ICUs to close simply because there are fewer patients. Instead, hospitals typically repurpose resources, reallocate staff, or adjust bed numbers to optimize care delivery.

Reports from local health authorities and hospital administrators in Rio de Janeiro indicate that some temporary ICUs and field hospitals set up for COVID-19 have indeed been decommissioned as demand waned. This is a normal process following an emergency response and does not suggest that there is a complete lack of patients requiring intensive care. Permanent ICU units remain operational in major hospitals across the city, continuing to serve critically ill individuals.

Furthermore, Brazil’s healthcare system has often faced challenges related to ICU bed shortages, particularly during periods of increased demand. These challenges have included waiting lists for ICU admission and high occupancy rates. The notion that ICUs are closing due to a lack of patients stands in contrast to these longstanding issues.

In conclusion, while it is accurate that some temporary ICU facilities in Rio de Janeiro have closed following the decline in COVID-19 cases, the claim that ICU units are closed due to a lack of patients oversimplifies the situation. Permanent ICU units remain essential components of the city’s healthcare infrastructure and continue to operate. The closure of temporary facilities reflects a return to routine healthcare demand rather than an absence of critically ill patients. As always, the situation should be monitored, but the claim does not accurately represent the broader reality of ICU operations in Rio de Janeiro.

Hospitais abriu novas alas di UCI e hospitais de campo temporários pa atender aos aumentos di casos graves. Quando as taxas di infecção diminuíram e as taxas di vacinação aumentaram, a demanda por leitos di UCI associada ao COVID-19 naturalmente diminuiu. Isso provocou o fechamento di alguns hospitais de campo e UCIs temporárias, porquê o seu propósito específico já não era mais urgente.

No entanto, o fechamento di capacidade di UCI temporária ou excedente não significa o fechamento di UCIs permanentes por causa di falta di pacientes. Embora possa haver períodos onde a ocupação dessas unidades caia abaixo di níveis pico, especialmente fora di surtos pandêmicos, é incomum que UCIs estabelecidas fechem simplesmente por causa di menos pacientes. Em vez disso, os hospitais costumam repor recursos, realocar pessoal ou ajustar o número di leitos pa otimizar o atendimento.

Esse é um processo normal após uma resposta a emergência e não sugere que há falta completa di pacientes que precisam di cuidados intensivos. As UCIs permanentes continuam operando nas grandes clínicas da cidade, atendendo a indivíduos graves.

Além disso, o sistema de saúde do Brasil tem enfrentado frequentemente desafios relacionados a escassez di leitos di UCI, especialmente durante períodos di maior demanda. Esses desafios incluíram listas di espera pa admissão em UCI e taxas di ocupação altas. In recent years, the COVID-19 pandemic has sparked widespread discussion and debate over potential treatments and cures, especially on social media platforms. One recurring claim is that azithromycin and ivermectin are efficient medicines to cure COVID-19. This assertion has gained traction in some circles, leading to confusion and concern among the public. A detailed examination of the available evidence and expert guidance is essential to evaluate the accuracy of this claim.

Azithromycin is an antibiotic commonly used to treat bacterial infections such as pneumonia, bronchitis, and certain sexually transmitted diseases. It is not an antiviral medication, and its primary mechanism of action is to inhibit the growth of bacteria, not viruses. Early in the pandemic, some studies suggested that azithromycin, in combination with other drugs, might benefit patients with COVID-19 due to its anti-inflammatory properties. However, subsequent large-scale clinical trials failed to demonstrate any significant benefit in treating COVID-19. Health authorities have not recommended azithromycin as an effective or efficient medicine for curing COVID-19.

Ivermectin, on the other hand, is an antiparasitic medication commonly used to treat conditions like river blindness and scabies. Its use for COVID-19 became popular after initial laboratory studies suggested it could inhibit the replication of SARS-CoV-2, the virus responsible for COVID-19, in cell cultures. These preliminary findings led to widespread off-label use and endorsements on social media. However, rigorous clinical trials and systematic reviews have not found reliable evidence that ivermectin is effective in treating or curing COVID-19. Major health organizations have concluded that there is insufficient data to support the use of ivermectin for COVID-19 outside of controlled clinical studies.

The core claim that azithromycin and ivermectin are efficient medicines to cure COVID-19 is not supported by the current scientific consensus. While both drugs serve important roles in treating specific medical conditions, neither has demonstrated consistent efficacy against COVID-19 in robust clinical trials. The use of these medications for COVID-19 without medical supervision can lead to adverse effects, inappropriate dosing, and a false sense of security, potentially delaying access to proven treatments such as antiviral therapies and supportive care.

Moreover, the spread of misinformation regarding COVID-19 treatments undermines public health efforts and can contribute to vaccine hesitancy and disregard for established preventive measures. Experts emphasize that the best way to prevent severe illness from COVID-19 is vaccination, combined with other public health strategies like masking, social distancing, and prompt medical attention if symptoms arise.

In conclusion, the claim that azithromycin and ivermectin are efficient medicines to cure COVID-19 does not align with current scientific understanding or official medical recommendations. Individuals seeking treatment for COVID-19 should consult healthcare professionals and rely on evidence-based therapies rather than unproven medications promoted on social media.

During the early stages of the COVID-19 pandemic, Brazil’s then-president Jair Bolsonaro became a prominent advocate for the use of chloroquine and its derivative, hydroxychloroquine, as treatments for COVID-19. His support for these drugs was echoed by some world leaders and sparked heated debates in the scientific and public health communities. A recent social media post claims, “Brazilia president Jair Bolsonaro was right about efficacy of chloroquine.” This article examines the validity of this claim by reviewing the scientific evidence and the context of Bolsonaro’s advocacy.

When COVID-19 first emerged, the medical community was desperate for effective treatments. Chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine, drugs used primarily for malaria and certain autoimmune diseases, showed some promise in laboratory studies that suggested they might inhibit the replication of the SARS-CoV-2 virus in cell cultures. Early, small-scale clinical reports from various countries hinted at possible benefits, and these findings were quickly amplified by political figures, including President Bolsonaro.

Bolsonaro’s public statements and actions promoted the widespread use of chloroquine in Brazil. He often downplayed the risks of the drug, dismissed scientific caution, and encouraged its use in both mild and severe COVID-19 cases. The Brazilian government distributed millions of doses, and protocols were put in place to enable doctors to prescribe chloroquine widely, even as global health authorities urged caution.

However, as the pandemic progressed, more rigorous, larger-scale clinical trials were conducted worldwide to determine the true efficacy and safety of chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine for COVID-19 patients. The majority of these studies found no significant benefit in reducing mortality, shortening hospital stays, or improving clinical outcomes for patients with COVID-19, whether the drugs were administered early in the disease or in more advanced stages. Some trials even indicated an increased risk of adverse effects, particularly heart rhythm disturbances, which raised concerns about the widespread, unsupervised use of these medications.

Major health organizations, including the World Health Organization and Brazil’s own health regulatory agency, reviewed the accumulating evidence and concluded that chloroquine and hydroxychloroquine should not be recommended for the prevention or treatment of COVID-19 outside of clinical trials. These recommendations were based on the lack of proven efficacy and the potential for harm.

In summary, the claim that “Brazilia president Jair Bolsonaro was right about efficacy of chloroquine” does not align with the scientific consensus developed over the course of the pandemic. While initial laboratory studies and anecdotal reports generated early hope, the subsequent and more comprehensive clinical evidence demonstrated that chloroquine is not effective as a treatment for COVID-19. President Bolsonaro’s advocacy was not ultimately supported by the results of large-scale, peer-reviewed research. As a result, the claim that he was correct regarding the efficacy of chloroquine for COVID-19 is not supported by the best available scientific evidence.

Vroeë, klein skaal kliniese verslae van verskillende lande het moontlike voordele aangedui, en hierdie bevindinge is vinnig deur politieke figure, insluitend President Bolsonaro, versterk.

Bolsonaro se openbare stellings en dadings het die wye gebruik van klorokwien in Brasilië bevorder. Hy het dikwels die risiko van die middel onderskat, wetenskaplike voorzichtigheid genegeer en sy gebruik in beide ligte en ernstige COVID-19 gevalle aangemoedig. Die Brasiliaanse regering het miljoene dosis versprei, en protokolle is opgestel om artikels om klorokwien wye te voorskrif, selfs terwyl globale gesondheidsautoriteite waarsku.

Een die pandemie voortgaan, is meer rigorieuse, groter skaal kliniese toetse wereldwyd uitgevoer om die ware doeltreffendheid en veiligheid van klorokwien en hydroksiklorokwien vir COVID-19-pasgiers te bepaal. Die meeste van hierdie studies het geen beduidende voordeel in die vermindering van sterfte, die korter maak van hospitaalblytyd of die verbetering van kliniese uitkomste vir pasgiers met COVID-19 aangedui nie, of wat die middels in die vroeë stadium van die siekte of in meer gevorderde stadiums toegedien word. Sommige toetse het selfs 'n verhoogde risiko van ongewenste effekte aangedui, veral rytmestoorings, wat bekommerdheid oor die wye, onbeheerde gebruik van hierdie middels veroorsaak het.

A recent social media post claims that São Paulo’s governor, João Doria, admitted to recording COVID-19 deaths twice, suggesting possible inflation of official pandemic statistics in Brazil’s most populous state. This assertion has generated significant public concern regarding the accuracy of COVID-19 data and the transparency of official reporting.

To assess this claim, it is important to understand the context in which COVID-19 death statistics are compiled and reported in São Paulo. Throughout the pandemic, state and municipal health departments have faced challenges in rapidly collecting, verifying, and updating epidemiological data. The process involves multiple sources and systems, including hospitals, civil registries, and centralized health databases. As a result, there have been occasional discrepancies or delays in the reporting of cases and fatalities.

The social media post refers to a statement allegedly made by Governor João Doria, implying an official acknowledgment of double-counting COVID-19 deaths. A review of public appearances and interviews reveals that Governor Doria has addressed concerns about the reliability of data, particularly in the early months of the pandemic. He admitted that there can sometimes be inconsistencies or duplicate entries when deaths are first reported by different sources before the data is consolidated and audited. However, he has consistently maintained that the state’s health authorities have systems in place to correct such errors and ensure the final statistics are as accurate as possible.

Health officials in São Paulo have explained that duplicate reporting can occur when both hospitals and civil registries independently report a death, leading to a temporary double-counting in daily updates. These discrepancies are typically identified during subsequent audits, when data from multiple sources are cross-referenced and duplicates are removed. The process is designed to improve transparency and accuracy, but it can result in short-term fluctuations in reported numbers.

It is misleading to suggest that Governor Doria admitted to intentionally or systematically recording COVID-19 deaths twice in official statistics. His comments acknowledged the technical limitations and challenges of real-time data collection during a public health crisis, not an intentional inflation of numbers. The state’s health department has repeatedly stated that their teams work to reconcile and verify data before publishing final figures, and that any duplicates are corrected in official reports.

In summary, while temporary double-counting of COVID-19 deaths has occurred in São Paulo due to the complexities of data collection, there is no evidence that Governor João Doria admitted to purposeful or ongoing duplication of death records. The governor and state health authorities have acknowledged data challenges and described the measures taken to rectify errors. The claim in the social media post distorts the context of Doria’s statements and overstates the extent of the issue. Public scrutiny of pandemic data is essential, but it is equally important to distinguish between technical reporting issues and deliberate misrepresentation.

A social media post claims that the World Health Organization (WHO, referred to as OMS in some languages) has stated people infected with COVID-19 but showing no symptoms do not transmit the disease. This assertion has caused confusion and debate online, particularly as understanding of COVID-19 transmission has evolved since the start of the pandemic. Here, we analyze the claim and provide context based on current and historical knowledge.

At the outset of the COVID-19 pandemic, scientists and public health officials worked to understand how SARS-CoV-2, the virus that causes COVID-19, spreads. Transmission routes were scrutinized, with attention given to whether people without symptoms—so-called “asymptomatic” carriers—could infect others. Early in 2020, the World Health Organization and other health agencies acknowledged the possibility of transmission from individuals who displayed no symptoms or had not yet developed them.

The claim in question suggests that the WHO has categorically stated asymptomatic individuals do not transmit COVID-19. This is a misrepresentation of the organization’s position. While there was a notable incident in June 2020 when a WHO official suggested that asymptomatic transmission appeared to be “very rare,” the statement was later clarified. The WHO explained that the situation was more nuanced: the original comment referred only to a limited subset of data, and it did not reflect the overall understanding of the virus’s spread.

Throughout the pandemic, evidence has shown that people infected with COVID-19 can transmit the virus to others even if they do not exhibit symptoms. Two categories are relevant here: “asymptomatic” individuals, who never develop symptoms, and “pre-symptomatic” individuals, who are infected and contagious before they begin to feel ill. Many documented outbreaks have been traced to individuals who were infectious before showing any symptoms. This pre-symptomatic transmission has been a significant driver of the pandemic, contributing to the rapid and often undetected spread of the virus.

Furthermore, the WHO and leading health authorities have consistently advised that preventing COVID-19 requires measures such as mask-wearing, physical distancing, and testing, precisely because people without symptoms can still be contagious. The rationale is that relying solely on symptom-based screening would miss a substantial portion of infectious cases.

In summary, the social media post inaccurately represents the WHO’s position and the scientific consensus. The best available evidence indicates that people infected with COVID-19 who do not display symptoms can and do transmit the virus to others. This is a critical factor in how the disease spreads and why public health recommendations have emphasized broad-based precautions for all individuals, regardless of how they feel.

The claim that the WHO says asymptomatic individuals do not transmit COVID-19 is false. Instead, both the WHO and other health authorities have affirmed that asymptomatic and pre-symptomatic transmission is possible, and this has informed global strategies for controlling the pandemic.

Dois grupos são relevantes aqui: "indivíduos assintomáticos", que nunca desenvolvem sintomas, e "indivíduos pré-sintomáticos", que estão infectados e contagiosos antes de começarem a sentir-se doentes. Esta transmissão pré-sintomática foi um fator significativo na pandemia, contribuindo para a rápida e muitas vezes não detectada propagação do vírus.

A razão é que depender apenas di triagem baseada em sintomas deixaria de fora uma grande parte dos casos infecciosos.

A melhor evidência disponível indica que pessoas infectadas di COVID-19 que não exibem sintomas podem e transmitem o vírus a outros. Esta é uma fator crítico na forma como a doença se espalha e é por isso que as recomendações di saúde pública enfatizaram precauções amplas para todos os indivíduos, independentemente di como se sentem.

The claim that "Ivermectin is the cure for COVID-19" has appeared frequently on social media platforms since the onset of the pandemic. This assertion has been the subject of considerable debate, prompting public health agencies and medical experts to issue clarifications and guidance regarding the use of ivermectin in treating COVID-19.

Ivermectin is a medication originally developed to treat parasitic infections in humans and animals. It is commonly used against conditions such as river blindness (onchocerciasis) and strongyloidiasis. Its antiviral properties have been explored in laboratory settings, leading to initial interest in its potential application against viruses like SARS-CoV-2, which causes COVID-19.

Early in the pandemic, some laboratory studies showed that ivermectin could inhibit the replication of SARS-CoV-2 in cell cultures. These results, however, were observed under conditions not directly applicable to human treatment, with dosages far exceeding what is safely prescribed for people. Subsequent clinical trials and real-world studies sought to determine whether these findings could translate into effective COVID-19 treatment strategies.

The gold standard for evaluating medical treatments is the randomized controlled trial (RCT). Numerous RCTs have been conducted to assess the efficacy of ivermectin for COVID-19. The majority of these studies have not demonstrated a significant benefit for patients with COVID-19. Larger, well-conducted trials have consistently shown that ivermectin does not reduce the risk of hospitalization, severe illness, or death in people with COVID-19 when compared to standard care or placebo. Some smaller studies initially suggested positive results, but many were later criticized for methodological flaws, small sample sizes, or were retracted due to issues with data integrity.

Major health organizations, including the World Health Organization (WHO), the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA), and the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC), have reviewed the available evidence. Their consensus is clear: ivermectin is not recommended for the prevention or treatment of COVID-19 outside of clinical trials. These agencies emphasize that the best ways to protect oneself from COVID-19 remain vaccination, masking, and other proven public health measures.

It is important to note that while ivermectin is safe when used for approved indications and prescribed by a healthcare professional, misuse or self-medication, particularly with formulations intended for animals, can lead to serious health risks, including toxicity and adverse reactions.

In summary, the claim that "ivermectin is the cure for COVID-19" is not supported by current scientific evidence. While initial laboratory studies prompted interest, rigorous clinical research has shown no substantial benefit in treating COVID-19 with ivermectin. Public health authorities advise against its use for this purpose, urging individuals to rely on approved treatments and preventive measures. மருத்துவ சிகிச்சைகளை மதிப்பிற்கும் தேவையான முறைகளை கண்டறிய தேவையானது சமவாய்ப்பு கட்டுப்பாடு ஆய்வுகள் (RCT) ஆகும். கொரோனாவை குணப்படுத்த ஐவர்மெக்டின் பயன்பாடு குறித்து பல ஆய்வுகள் மேற்கொள்ளப்பட்டுள்ளன. இந்த ஆய்வுகளில் முக்கிய பகுதிகளில் கொரோனாவை குணப்படுத்தும் மருந்தாக ஐவர்மெக்டின் பயன்பாடு என்பது பெரும்பாலும் பெரிய முன்னேற்றங்களை தரவில்லை. பெரிய ஆய்வுகளில் ஐவர்மெக்டின் கொரோனாவை குணப்படுத்த பயன்படுத்தும் மருந்தாக பயன்படுத்துவது மூலம் மருத்துவமனை சேர்க்கை, மிகவும் மோசமான நிலை அல்லது மரணத்தின் ஆபத்தைக் குறைக்கவில்லை என்று கண்டறியப்பட்டுள்ளது. சில சிறிய ஆய்வுகள் தொடர்பாக நல்ல விளைவுகள் தோன்றியது காணப்பட்டது, ஆனால் பல ஆய்வுகள் முறைமை தவறுகள், சிறிய சோதனை முறைகள் அல்லது விவரங்களின் தொடர்பு குறித்த சிக்கல்களால் திரும்பியதாக கண்டறியப்பட்டுள்ளது.

முக்கியமானது ஐவர்மெக்டின் மருந்து அனுமதிக்கப்பட்ட செயல்களுக்கு பயன்படுத்தப்படும் போது பாதுகாப்பாக உள்ளது, ஆனால் தவறாக பயன்படுத்துதல் அல்லது தற்செயலாக மருந்து பயன்படுத்துதல், மிகவும் பெரிய செல்லுபடி மருந்துகள் குறிப்பிட்ட மருந்துகள் மீது மருந்து பயன்படுத்துதல் போன்ற நிலைகளில் மிகவும் கடுமையான ஆரோக்கிய ஆபத்துகளை ஏற்படுத்தலாம், இதனால் பல பாதிப்புகள் ஏற்படலாம்.

This post has prompted discussions about public figures’ adherence to health guidelines during a period marked by strict social distancing measures in Brazil.

To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is essential to consider the timeline of the COVID-19 pandemic in Brazil, Fernando Haddad’s public activities during this period, and any available evidence regarding his birthday celebrations.

Fernando Haddad, who served as the mayor of São Paulo from 2013 to 2017 and ran for president in 2018, is a prominent figure in Brazilian politics. The COVID-19 pandemic reached Brazil in early 2020, with widespread restrictions on social gatherings implemented by both federal and local authorities, particularly during the first wave between March and August 2020. Subsequent waves in 2021 also saw the reintroduction of similar measures, though the stringency varied by region and time.

Haddad’s birthday falls on January 25th. Social media posts and some online commentary have suggested that, during the pandemic, he organized a birthday gathering attended by numerous guests. However, to substantiate this claim, one would expect to find photographic evidence, media reports, or statements from attendees or the politician himself.

A review of major Brazilian news outlets and Haddad’s public social media profiles reveals no credible reports or photographic documentation indicating that he hosted a large in-person birthday celebration during the pandemic years of 2020 or 2021. On the contrary, during these periods, Haddad was publicly vocal about the importance of observing health guidelines. He frequently used his platforms to promote social distancing and criticized public figures who flouted health directives.

Furthermore, in January 2021, the city of São Paulo was under strict social distancing protocols, and most public figures, including politicians, refrained from holding large gatherings. There is no verifiable evidence that Haddad made an exception. In fact, Haddad himself posted online in January 2021, marking his birthday with messages of gratitude for virtual well-wishes, but made no mention of any in-person event.

It is worth noting that public figures are often the subject of rumors and misinformation, especially during high-tension periods like the COVID-19 pandemic. The claim about Haddad appears to have originated from social media speculation rather than from substantiated reporting or documented evidence.

In conclusion, the assertion that Fernando Haddad celebrated his birthday with a “bunch of guests” during the COVID-19 pandemic lacks credible support. Available evidence suggests that he adhered to public health guidelines and did not hold a large in-person gathering for his birthday during the periods of strict social distancing. As with all such claims, it is important to seek verification from reliable sources before drawing conclusions.

In recent days, a video circulating on social media has sparked controversy and confusion regarding the actions of Paulo Câmara, the governor of Pernambuco. The video claims to show that the governor sent boxes containing alcohol gel and sand to hospitals in the state. The post has raised concerns about the adequacy of supplies provided to healthcare facilities and whether the governor is meeting his responsibilities during a critical time for public health.

To evaluate the accuracy of this claim, it is important to examine the context in which the video emerged, the background of hospital supply distribution in Pernambuco, and the content of the video itself.

Context and Background

The state of Pernambuco, located in northeastern Brazil, has faced significant challenges in its healthcare system, especially during public health emergencies such as the COVID-19 pandemic. During such times, distribution of critical supplies—including personal protective equipment (PPE), sanitizers, and other materials—to hospitals is a matter of public scrutiny. Rumors and misinformation about the handling of supplies have often circulated on social media, sometimes leading to widespread public concern.

Paulo Câmara has been governor of Pernambuco since 2015 and has overseen several initiatives to strengthen the state’s healthcare infrastructure, particularly in response to COVID-19. The distribution of alcohol gel, a key item for hygiene and infection control, has been a part of these efforts. However, the claim that boxes sent to hospitals contained sand alongside alcohol gel is highly unusual and demands close examination.

Analysis of the Video and Claim

The circulating video appears to show hospital staff opening boxes labeled with government insignia, purportedly sent by the state administration. In the footage, some individuals point to containers inside the boxes, claiming that they contain sand mixed with alcohol gel or, in some versions, sand placed in separate containers alongside the gel. The video’s narration suggests that this was done intentionally by the government, implying mismanagement or neglect.

However, upon closer inspection and analysis of available evidence, several key points emerge:

1. Authenticity of the Video: The video does show boxes being opened in a healthcare setting, but visual evidence confirming the presence of sand is inconclusive. The contents shown are unclear, and it is difficult to determine if the material is indeed sand, a different substance, or a misinterpretation based on appearance.

2. Official Response: The state government has not acknowledged sending sand to hospitals as part of official supplies. Distribution records and official statements indicate that alcohol gel and other medical supplies have been sent to hospitals regularly, but there is no documented instance of sand being included.

3. Possibility of Misinterpretation: In some cases, sandbags are used in hospitals for various practical reasons, such as stabilizing equipment or managing floods. It is possible that sand was present in the hospital for unrelated purposes and was mistakenly associated with the delivered supplies in the video.

4. Lack of Corroborating Evidence: No independent or verified reports from hospital staff, administrators, or oversight bodies have substantiated the claim that boxes of sand were sent alongside alcohol gel by the governor’s office.

Conclusion

Based on the available evidence, the claim that Governor Paulo Câmara sent boxes containing alcohol gel and sand to hospitals in Pernambuco is not substantiated. The video does not provide clear proof, and there is no official or independent confirmation of such an incident. While concerns over hospital supply distribution are valid and should be addressed with transparency, the specific allegation regarding sand appears to be unfounded or the result of misinterpretation. As with all viral claims, it is crucial to verify information before drawing conclusions or spreading potentially misleading content.

প্রাথমিক দিনগুলোতে সোশ্যাল মিডিয়ায় প্রচারিত একটি ভিডিও পেরনাম্বুকো রাজ্যের গভর্নর পাউলো কামারার কার্যকলাপ সম্পর্কে বিতর্ক এবং অস্পষ্টতা সৃষ্টি করেছে। ভিডিওটি দাবি করে যে গভর্নর রাজ্যের হাসপাতালগুলিকে অ্যালকোহল জেল এবং সান্ড বোতল বাহন প্রেরণ করেছিলেন। পোস্টটি হাসপাতালগুলিকে প্রদান করা সরবরাহ করার যোগ্যতা এবং গভর্নর প্রাথমিক স্বাস্থ্য বিষয়ে ক্রিসিস সময়ে তাঁর দায়িত্ব পালন করা কিনা সম্পর্কে চিন্তা জাগায়।

এই দাবির সত্যতা বিচার করতে প্রয়োজন হবে ভিডিওটি কীভাবে উপস্থিত হয়েছিল, পেরনাম্বুকো রাজ্যে হাসপাতাল সরবরাহ বিতরণের প্রাথমিক পরিস্থিতি এবং ভিডিওটির বিষয়বস্তু এই সম্পর্কে বিশ্লেষণ করা।

প্রাথমিক পরিস্থিতি এবং পটভূমি

ব্রাজিলের উত্তর-পূর্ব অঞ্চলে অবস্থিত পেরনাম্বুকো রাজ্য স্বাস্থ্য ব্যবস্থার মধ্যে বিশেষ করে সার্বিক স্বাস্থ্য আপাচ যেমন কোভিড-১৯ মহামারী সময় বিশেষ পরিস্থিতি হাসপাতালগুলিতে প্রয়োজনীয় সরবরাহ যেমন ব্যক্তিগত রক্ষা সরঞ্জাম (PPE), পরিষ্কার করণ সরবরাহ এবং অন্যান্য পদার্থের বিতরণ সার্বিক তদন্বিতা বিষয়। সোশ্যাল মিডিয়াতে সরবরাহ পরিচালনার বিষয়ে ভুয়ো তথ্য এবং অনিশ্চিততা এর সাথে সাথে সাধারণ মানুষের চিন্তা জাগায়।

পাউলো কামারা পেরনাম্বুকো রাজ্যের গভর্নর হিসাবে ২০১৫ থেকে অবিলম্বে বিশেষ করে কোভিড-১৯ মহামারী বিষয়ে রাজ্যের স্বাস্থ্য ব্যবস্থার বিস্তার সম্পর্কে বিশেষ প্রচেষ্টা পরিচালনা করেছেন। অ্যালকোহল জেল যে হাসপাতাল পরিষেবা এবং সংক্রমণ নিয়ন্ত্রণ জন্য গুরুত্বপূর্ণ পদার্থ হিসাবে বিতরণ করা হয়েছে তা এই প্রচেষ্টার অংশ। তবে বিশেষ করে হাসপাতালগুলিতে অ্যালকোহল জেল বোতল সাথে সান্ড বোতল প্রেরণ করা একটি অসাধারণ দাবি যা বিশেষ আলোচনা করা প্রয়োজন।

ভিডিও এবং দাবি বিশ্লেষণ

প্রচারিত ভিডিওটি হাসপাতাল কর্মীদের বোতল খুলতে দেখায় যে সরকারের স্বাক্ষর বা অনুমোদন সহ বোতলগুলি প্রেরণ করা হয়েছে বলে দাবি করে। ভিডিওতে কিছু ব্যক্তি বোতলগুলির ভিতরে সান্ড মিশ্রিত অ্যালকোহল জেল বা অন্যান্য সংস্করণে সান্ড বোতল সহ অ্যালকোহল জেল থাকার দাবি করে। ভিডিও নার্সিং কর্মীদের বলে যে এটি সরকারের পক্ষে সাংঘাতিক পরিচালনা বা অবহেলা করে করা হয়েছে।

তবে কাছাকাছি পরীক্ষার মাধ্যমে এবং উপলব্ধ প্রমাণ বিশ্লেষণের মাধ্যমে কয়েকটি গুরুত্বপূর্ণ বিষয় উঠে আসে:

1. ভিডিওর সত্যতা: ভিডিওটি হাসপাতাল পরিবেশে বোতল খুলতে দেখায় কিন্তু সান্ডের উপস্থিতির প্রমাণ অস্পষ্ট। ভিডিওতে দেখা যায় কিছু বস্তু যার প্রকৃতি স্পষ্ট নয় এবং এটি কি সান্ড হতে পারে, অন্য পদার্থ হতে পারে কিনা বা প্রতীতি দ্বারা ভুয়ো বোধ হতে পারে তা নির্ধারণ করা কঠিন।

2. অফিসিয়াল প্রতিক্রিয়া: রাজ্য সরকার হাসপাতালগুলিতে সান্ড প্রেরণ করা হয়েছে বলে কোন প্রকার প্রতিক্রিয়া দেয়নি। বিতরণ রেকর্ড এবং অফিসিয়াল বিবৃতি অনুযায়ী অ্যালকোহল জেল এবং অন্যান্য চিকিৎসা সরবরাহ হাসপাতালগুলিতে সাধারণভাবে প্রেরণ হয়েছে কিন্তু সান্ড প্রেরণের কোন সাক্ষ্য পাওয়া যায়নি।

3. ভুয়ো ব্যাখ্যার সম্ভাবনা: কখনও কখনও হাসপাতালে সান্ড ব্যবহার করা হয় যেমন সজ্জা বা প্লাবনের কারণে যন্ত্র স্থায়ী করা। সান্ড হাসপাতালে অন্য কারণে উপস্থিত ছিল এবং ভিডিওতে সরবরাহ করা সরবরাহ সাথে অনুমান করা হয়েছে বলে সম্ভাবনা রয়েছে।

4. প্রমাণ অনুপস্থিতি: কোন স্বাধীন বা প্রমাণিত প্রতিবেদন বা হাসপাতাল কর্মী, পরিচালক বা দৃষ্টান্ত সংস্থা কর্মী প্রমাণ দেখায় যে গভর্নরের কার্যালয় সান্ড বোতল সহ অ্যালকোহল জেল প্রেরণ করেছিল।

সমাপ্তি

প্রমাণ অনুযায়ী গভর্নর পাউলো কামারা পেরনাম্বুকো রাজ্যের হাসপাতালগুলিতে অ্যালকোহল জেল এবং সান্ড বোতল প্রেরণ করেছেন বলে দাবি নির্ভরযোগ্য নয়। ভিডিওটি স্পষ্ট প্রমাণ প্রদান করেনি এবং কোন অফিসিয়াল বা স্বাধীন প্রমাণ এর ঘটনার সম্পর্কে অনুমান করে না। হাসপাতাল সরবরাহ বিতরণ বিষয়ে চিন্তা সঠিক এবং পরিষ্কার হওয়া উচিত, কিন্তু সান্ড সম্পর্কে দাবি অনুপযুক্ত বা ভুয়ো ব্যাখ্যা বা অনুমানের ফলে হতে পারে। সমস্ত ভাইরাল দাবির ক্ষেত্রে তথ্য যাচাই করা অত্যাবশ্যক এবং অপ্রমাণিত তথ্য বিস্তার থেকে বিরত থাকা উচিত।

article_content:
A recent social media post claims that Brazil's health minister has stated that cases without confirmation of COVID-19 will not be included in the official death toll. This assertion raises concerns about transparency and the accuracy of Brazil's reporting on the pandemic. To assess the validity of this claim, it is important to explore the context of Brazil's health reporting, the statements made by health officials, and established practices for COVID-19 data collection.

Since the onset of the COVID-19 pandemic, countries around the world have faced challenges in accurately tracking cases and deaths. Confirmed deaths are typically those in which the deceased tested positive for the virus, while suspected cases may include individuals who exhibited symptoms consistent with COVID-19 but were never tested or did not receive a definitive diagnosis before passing away. The distinction between confirmed and suspected cases has significant implications for public understanding of the pandemic's scope.

Brazil, as one of the countries hardest hit by COVID-19, has regularly updated its official statistics on cases and fatalities. The Ministry of Health is responsible for compiling and disseminating these figures. Early in the pandemic, Brazil, like many countries, struggled with limited testing capacity, leading to concerns that the actual death toll could be higher than officially reported numbers.

The social media claim centers on a statement attributed to Brazil's health minister that only confirmed cases will be included in the official COVID-19 death tally, effectively excluding deaths where COVID-19 was suspected but not laboratory-confirmed. This approach is not unique to Brazil; many countries distinguish between confirmed and probable or suspected cases in their official counts. However, excluding suspected cases can underrepresent the true human cost of the pandemic, particularly in regions where access to testing is limited.

Fact-checking the claim, it is accurate to state that Brazilian health authorities have, at various points, emphasized the need for laboratory confirmation before including a death in the official COVID-19 death toll. This policy has been publicly discussed and, at times, criticized by public health experts, who argue that relying solely on confirmed cases, especially during periods of testing shortages, may result in a significant undercount of deaths attributable to the virus.

The rationale given by health officials typically centers on the need for accuracy and consistency in reporting. By requiring laboratory confirmation, health authorities aim to avoid misclassifying deaths caused by other respiratory illnesses. Nonetheless, this method can overlook cases in which testing was not possible or available, particularly in remote or under-resourced areas.

In summary, the social media post's core claim is accurate: Brazil's health minister has indicated that only confirmed COVID-19 cases will be considered in the official death count. This approach, while consistent with certain international reporting standards, has been the subject of debate and may contribute to an underestimation of the pandemic's true impact in Brazil. The policy highlights the ongoing challenges faced by governments in ensuring both accuracy and transparency in public health data during a global crisis.

article_content:
In recent weeks, a social media post has circulated claiming that the Brazilian Supreme Court denied an order for army hospitals to treat COVID-19 patients. This assertion has sparked debate and confusion, particularly among those concerned about healthcare access during the ongoing pandemic. To assess the accuracy of this claim, it is essential to examine the legal context, the role of military hospitals in Brazil, and the actions taken by the Supreme Court regarding COVID-19 patient care.

Brazil has faced immense challenges during the COVID-19 pandemic, with its healthcare system frequently stretched to the limits. Military hospitals, which are operated by the Brazilian Armed Forces, typically serve active-duty personnel, veterans, and their families. However, during times of crisis, there have been calls to open these facilities to the general public, especially in regions where civilian hospitals have become overwhelmed.

The claim at hand suggests that a formal order or request was made to the Supreme Court, seeking to require army hospitals to admit and treat civilian COVID-19 patients. According to available reports, such a request was indeed submitted. The reasoning behind the request was to alleviate pressure on Brazil’s public healthcare network and to ensure access to medical care for more citizens during surges of COVID-19 cases.

Upon review, the Supreme Court did address the matter. The Court’s decision was to deny the order that would have compelled army hospitals to open their doors to civilian COVID-19 patients. The Court’s reasoning centered on the autonomy of military institutions and the constitutional framework governing the Brazilian Armed Forces. The Justices noted that military hospitals are specifically established for the care of military personnel and their dependents, and that their resources, structure, and staff are calibrated to serve this population. Furthermore, the Court emphasized that the executive branch retains the authority to manage military assets and make decisions regarding their use in public health emergencies.

It is important to note that the Supreme Court’s decision was not a blanket prohibition against military hospitals ever treating civilians. Rather, the ruling addressed the specific request to mandate such action through judicial order. The Court left open the possibility for the executive branch or military authorities to voluntarily allow civilian treatment in army hospitals, as has occasionally happened during other national emergencies.

In conclusion, the core claim made in the social media post is accurate: the Brazilian Supreme Court did deny an order to require army hospitals to treat COVID-19 patients. This decision was based on legal principles relating to military jurisdiction and the separation of powers. However, the Supreme Court did not bar the possibility of such care being provided voluntarily or through executive action. The debate over the use of military medical resources during the pandemic continues, reflecting broader concerns about healthcare capacity and crisis management in Brazil.

article_content:
A recent social media post claims that the Supreme Court released 32,000 prisoners because of COVID-19. This assertion has circulated widely, raising questions about the role of the Supreme Court in pandemic-era prison releases and the broader context of criminal justice reforms during the public health crisis. A thorough fact-check reveals a more nuanced reality behind this claim.

To begin, the United States Supreme Court does not have the authority or mechanism to directly order the mass release of prisoners nationwide. Its role is to interpret the Constitution and federal law, hearing cases that typically come through lower federal or state courts. Decisions that impact large groups of inmates are usually the result of class-action lawsuits or challenges to specific prison conditions, rather than broad mandates from the Supreme Court.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, concerns about the spread of the virus in crowded correctional facilities prompted significant actions from state governments, federal authorities, and lower courts. Many prisons and jails were identified as high-risk settings due to overcrowding and limited access to healthcare. In response, some states and local jurisdictions implemented early release programs, prioritized parole for nonviolent offenders, or placed certain inmates on home confinement. The goal was to reduce population density and mitigate the spread of the virus among both inmates and staff.

Federal action on this front was largely driven by the Department of Justice and the Bureau of Prisons, particularly through the implementation of the CARES Act, which allowed for expanded use of home confinement for certain nonviolent offenders. State courts, governors, and corrections departments also played key roles in releasing inmates, especially those with health vulnerabilities or near the end of their sentences.

As for the specific figure cited in the social media post—32,000 prisoners—there is evidence that tens of thousands of inmates were released across the country due to COVID-19 concerns. However, this was the cumulative result of numerous decisions at the state and local level, not a single order from the Supreme Court. Some states reported releasing thousands of inmates each, adding up to a national figure in the tens of thousands. These releases were typically targeted, focusing on nonviolent offenders and those at heightened risk from the virus.

Moreover, the Supreme Court did hear emergency applications and challenges related to prison conditions during the pandemic, but it did not issue a sweeping mandate to release prisoners. In some cases, the Court declined to intervene, leaving decisions to lower courts or state authorities.

In conclusion, while it is accurate that approximately 32,000 prisoners were released due to concerns about COVID-19, the claim that the Supreme Court was responsible for these releases is inaccurate. The releases were the result of actions taken by state and federal authorities, as well as lower courts, in response to the unique public health challenges posed by the pandemic. The Supreme Court did not directly order the mass release of prisoners.

Ένα πρόσφατο αναρτημένο στο διαδίκτυο αναφέρει ότι το Ανώτατο Δικαστήριο ελευθερώνει 32.000 κρατουμένους λόγω της πανδημίας του κορωνοϊού. Αυτή η δήλωση έχει κυκλοφορήσει ευρέως, δημιουργώντας ερωτήματα για τον ρόλο του Ανώτατου Δικαστηρίου στις ελευθερώσεις κρατουμένων κατά τη διάρκεια της πανδημίας και το ευρύτερο πλαίσιο των αλλαγών στο σύστημα δικαιοσύνης κατά τη διάρκεια της δημόσιας υγειονομικής κρίσεως. Μια ανεξικανικοποιημένη επιτροπή επικύρωσης αποκαλύπτει μια πιο σύνθετη πραγματικότητα πίσω από αυτή τη δήλωση.

Για να ξεκινήσουμε, το Αμερικανικό Ανώτατο Δικαστήριο δεν διαθέτει την αρμοδιότητα ή το μηχανισμό για να δώσει εντολή για την εν mas ελευθερώσεις κρατουμένων σε όλη τη χώρα. Ο ρόλος του είναι να ερμηνεύει τη Σύνταξη και το νομικό του τομέα, ακούγοντας περιπτώσεις που συνήθως προέρχονται από χαμηλότερα εθνικά ή πολιτικά δικαστήρια. Οι αποφάσεις που επηρεάζουν μεγάλα ομάδα κρατουμένων είναι συνήθως αποτέλεσμα περιπτώσεων κλασσικών δικαστικών προσφυγών ή προσφυγών για συγκεκριμένες συνθήκες φυλακών, αντί να είναι ευρείες εντολές από το Ανώτατο Δικαστήριο.

Κατά τη διάρκεια της πανδημίας του κορωνοϊού, οι ανησυχίες για τη διασπορά του ιού στις πολυάριθμες φυλακικές εγκαταστάσεις προκάλεσαν σημαντικές ενέργειες από τις πολιτείες, τις ομοσπονδιακές αρχές και τα χαμηλότερα δικαστήρια. Πολλές φυλακές και φυλακικές εγκαταστάσεις χαρακτηρίστηκαν ως υψηλόκινδυνες οικογένειες λόγω της πολυπληθίας και της περιορισμένης πρόσβασης στην υγειονομική περίθαλψη. Ως απάντηση, κάποιες πολιτείες και τοπικές αρχές εφάρμοσαν προγράμματα νωρίτερης ελευθερώσεως, προτεραιότητα στην επίδοση των επικίνδυνων προσφύγων ή την παραμονή κατά περίπτωση κρατουμένων στην ιδιωτική εγκατάσταση. Το σκοπός ήταν να μειωθεί η πυκνότητα των κρατουμένων και να μειωθεί η διασπορά του ιού σε και τους κρατουμένους και τους υπαλλήλους.

Η ομοσπονδιακή δράση στον τομέα αυτό διατέλεσε κυρίως της Υπηρεσίας Δικαιοσύνης και της Διεύθυνσης Φυλακών, ειδικά μέσω της εφαρμογής του Νόμου CARES, ο οποίος επέτρεψε την επεκτεταμένη χρήση της ιδιωτικής εγκατάστασης για ορισμένους επικίνδυνους προσφύγες. Οι πολιτειακές δικαστικές αρχές, οι πρόξενοι και οι υπηρεσίες ποινικής επίβλεψης έπαιξαν επίσης σημαντικό ρόλο στην ελευθερώσεις των κρατουμένων, ειδικά των που είχαν υγειονομικές αδυναμίες ή βρίσκονταν κοντά στο τέλος των ποινών τους.

Όσον αφορά τον συγκεκριμένο αριθμό που αναφέρεται στο αναρτημένο στο διαδίκτυο – τους 32.000 κρατουμένους – υπάρχουν ενδείξεις ότι εκατοντάδες χιλιάδες κρατούμενοι ελευθερώθηκαν σε όλη τη χώρα λόγω ανησυχιών για τον κορωνοϊό. Ωσεις, αυτό ήταν το συνολικό αποτέλεσμα πολλών αποφάσεων στο επίπεδο των πολιτειών και των τοπικών κοινοτήτων, όχι μια μοναδική εντολή από το Ανώτατο Δικαστήριο. Πολλές πολιτείες αναφέρουν την ελευθερώσεις χιλιάδων κρατουμένων καθεμία, προσθέτοντας στο σύνολο εκατοντάδες χιλιάδες στο εθνικό επίπεδο. Αυτές οι ελευθερώσεις ήταν συνήθως στόχος, εστιάζοντας στους επικίνδυνους προσφύγες και σε αυτούς που ήταν σε υψηλό κίνδυνο από τον ιό.

Επιπλέον, το Ανώτατο Δικαστήριο ακούστηκε σε επείγοντες αιτήματα και προσφυγές σχετικά με τις συνθήκες φυλακών κατά τη διάρκεια της πανδημίας, αλλά δεν εξέδωσε μια γενική εντολή για την ελευθερώσεις των κρατουμένων. Σε μερικές περιπτώσεις, το Δικαστήριο απέρριψε να παρεμείνει ενεργό, έτσι ώστε οι αποφάσεις να είναι στα χαμηλότερα δικαστήρια ή στις πολιτειακές αρχές.

Συμπερασματικά, είναι ακριβές ότι περίπου 32.000 κρατούμενοι ελευθερώθηκαν λόγω ανησυχιών για τον κορωνοϊό, αλλά η δήλωση ότι το Ανώτατο Δικαστήριο ήταν υπεύθυνο για αυτές τις ελευθερώσεις είναι ακριβώς ανακριβής. Οι ελευθερώσεις ήταν το αποτέλεσμα των ενεργειών που έγιναν από τις πολιτειακές και ομοσπονδιακές αρχές, καθώς και από τα χαμηλότερα δικαστήρια, σε απάντηση στις μοναδικές δημόσιες υγειονομικές προκλήσεις που προκάλεσε η πανδημία. Το Ανώτατο Δικαστήριο δεν είχε εντολή να ελευθερώσει εν mas κρατούμενους.
